newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada proposes a land-mine ban before 1998.
newsitem.headline: Canada proposes a land-mine ban before 1998.

text.p: Fifty countries on Saturday adopted a declaration calling for the earliest possible agreement on a global ban on anti-personnel land mines.
But Canada's Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy went one step further, proposing a timetable for the signing of a treaty banning the mines.

"If the will is there, and we believe it is, we are offering to host an anti-personnel-mine ban treaty signing conference in December 1997 as a sign of our commitment to the ban," Axworthy said at the end of a three-day conference in Ottawa.

Axworthy's setting of a time target surprised and delighted many of the non-governmental organisations (NGOs) attending the conference, which had been expressing hope for a ban by 2000 at the beginning of the sessions on Thursday.
But few government representatives joined in the NGOs' standing ovation for Canada's proposal, perhaps indicating that it was too optimistic.
The declaration signed by participating countries does not mention a timetable for a global ban but sets out a series of steps that could lead to one.
These include supporting a United Nations General Assembly resolution calling for a ban on anti-personnel land mines, as well as developing regional activities working toward a ban.
The participants agreed to meet at a follow-up conference in Belgium next June to review progress.
The resolution was adopted at the end of the conference, which was organised by Canada with the aim of giving impetus to the fight against land mines.
Fifty nations took part fully, including the United States, Britain, France, Japan, Germany and Iran.
But some crucial nations did not sign the declaration, including Russia, China and most Middle Eastern countries.
Russia took part only as an observer, arguing that it was too early for it to agree to a total ban.

Russian representative Viatcheslav Sergueev told Reuters it was impossible for his government to agree to a ban, because an alternative to using land mines to protect nuclear plants and other possible terrorist targets had not yet been found.
But he said Russia would carefully examine the results of the conference before adopting a position on the issue.
China did not even attend the conference.
Many NGOs expressed optimism and satisfaction with the results of what they called a historic meeting.
"We have reached here the beginning of the end of anti-personnel land mines," Cornelio Sommaruga, president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, told a news conference.

About 500 people -- mostly civilians and many of them children -- are killed or maimed each week by anti-personnel mines, experts estimate. More than 110 million of the mines lurk under the soil in 70 countries.
